# Tecom Challenger

**Tecom Challenger** is an Australian family of electronic intrusion-alarm and access-control systems originally developed by **Tecom Systems** in Melbourne. The system combines alarm monitoring, user permissions, door access and, with suitable controllers, lift access. Its principal historical markets are Australia and New Zealand. ([1](#reference-1), [30](#reference-30))

Later commercial histories date the first Challenger release to **1989**. Surviving manufacturer documentation establishes Version 6 by September 1993 and places Version 8 in the mid-1990s. The principal later developments were **Challenger10** in 2013, **ChallengerPlus** in 2019 and **Tecom Discovery** in 2024. Discovery continues the Tecom system lineage under a different panel name. ([1](#reference-1), [2](#reference-2), [4](#reference-4), [7](#reference-7), [20](#reference-20), [24](#reference-24))

| Attribute | Details |
| --- | --- |
| Product type | Integrated intrusion-alarm and electronic access-control system |
| Country of origin | Australia |
| Original developer and manufacturer | Tecom Systems Pty Ltd, Melbourne |
| First introduction | 1989, according to retrospective integrator histories; an original launch announcement was not located |
| Main documented panel families | Challenger Version 6; Version 8; Challenger10; ChallengerSE; ChallengerLE; ChallengerPlus; ChallengerLEPlus |
| Later successor platform | Tecom Discovery, model TSX10000 |
| Brand and corporate group in September 2026 | Tecom within Aritech, part of Kidde Global Solutions |
| Principal historical markets | Australia and New Zealand |

*Scope: an encyclopedic history of the panel family and its associated hardware, software and ownership. Information checked to 3 September 2026. Sources and qualifications are provided below.*

## Origins and early development

Challenger originated with Tecom Systems in Melbourne. A retrospective account in *Security Electronics & Networks* credits **Dean Reilly and a team of electronics and software engineers** with developing Tecom's hardware and software. The available sources establish his central role but do not provide a complete account of the company's founders or initial financing. ([3](#reference-3))

Australian security integrators commonly give **1989** as Challenger's introduction year. This is useful as the reported beginning of the commercial product, although it should not be confused with the incorporation date of Tecom Systems or the release date of a particular numbered panel. ([1](#reference-1))

The original *Challenger Version 6 User Guide*, Issue III, is dated **September 1993**. Its manufacturer page identifies Tecom Systems Pty Ltd, ACN 005 523 562, at **8/36 New Street, Ringwood, Victoria**. This provides contemporary evidence of both the product and its Australian manufacturer. The Version 8 user guide published in October 1997 gives a later address at **646 Whitehorse Road, Mitcham, Victoria**. ([2](#reference-2), [8](#reference-8))

The early system already combined several functions that would remain characteristic of Challenger: independently controlled alarm areas, individual users, scheduled permissions, alarm-event history and access control. The Version 8 operating guide describes alarm groups, door groups, floor groups and time zones, showing that Challenger was an integrated building-security system by the 1990s. ([8](#reference-8))

## Panel generations

The dates below distinguish a confirmed release from the earliest dated evidence located. **“By” does not mean “launched in.”** A firmware version is also not necessarily a separate circuit board or commercial panel model.

| Period or date | Name | Identifying model or platform | Historical position |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1989, reported retrospectively | Original Challenger | Earliest model designation not established | Beginning of the commercial family in later integrator histories. ([1](#reference-1)) |
| By September 1993 | Challenger Version 6 | TS0015 | Early documented panel; an original Version 6 user manual survives. ([2](#reference-2), [5](#reference-5)) |
| 1990s; exact first release unverified | Version 7 | Documented as firmware for Version 6 hardware | Supported by period peripherals and later integration documentation. ([6](#reference-6), [7](#reference-7)) |
| By 1995 | Challenger Version 8 / Challenger V8 | TS0816 | Long-lived integrated alarm and access-control generation; a later Tecom manual cites an August 1995 V8 programming guide. ([7](#reference-7)) |
| 2013 | Challenger10 | TS1016 | Major processor, capacity and communications update to the V8 platform. ([4](#reference-4), [18](#reference-18)) |
| By August 2015 | ChallengerSE | TS1016SE | Standard Edition variant of the Challenger10 family, with reduced initial capacity and licensed expansion. ([19](#reference-19)) |
| By August 2015 | ChallengerLE | TS1016LE | Lite Edition, a smaller system with lower capacity. ([19](#reference-19)) |
| 9 September 2019 | ChallengerPlus | TS-CHPLUS / TS-CHPLUSB | Evolution of Challenger10, adding UltraSync and support for newer access-control equipment. ([20](#reference-20)) |
| By April 2021 | ChallengerLEPlus | TS1016LE in an earlier datasheet; TS1016LEPLUS in later documentation | Smaller Plus-era panel with UltraSync connectivity. ([22](#reference-22), [23](#reference-23)) |
| 26 August 2024 | Tecom Discovery | TSX10000 | New hardware platform with a web interface and DIN-rail housing. ([24](#reference-24)) |
| November 2025 | Discovery 2.0 | TSX-2 firmware on TSX10000 | Major firmware expansion of Discovery, rather than a separately identified panel model. ([25](#reference-25)) |

### Understanding the numbering

The public record does not establish a complete, consecutively marketed sequence from Challenger 1 through Challenger 10. Honeywell's documentation describes **Version 6 panels running Version 7 firmware**, illustrating why every version number cannot be treated as a different hardware generation. ([6](#reference-6))

Similarly, **ChallengerPlus uses V10-07-series firmware**, while Challenger10 continued on a V10-06 branch. Discovery uses a separate TSX firmware designation. Product names, board identifiers and firmware branches need to be distinguished when dating an installation. ([20](#reference-20), [26](#reference-26))

## Development of the panel family

### Version 6 and Version 7

Version 6 is among the earliest Challenger versions for which an original dated user manual remains publicly accessible. Tecom's TS0840 relay-card instructions identify the Version 6 control panel as **TS0015**, distinguishing it from the later **TS0816** Version 8 board. ([2](#reference-2), [5](#reference-5))

Version 7 appears in both peripheral documentation and third-party integration support. Tecom's November 1998 TS2053 radio-interface installation guide supports Version 7 and Version 8 panels and specifies corresponding firmware branches, including 7.64 MFR and 8.64 MFR. Honeywell's later documentation clarifies that a supported Version 7 configuration used Version 6 hardware. ([6](#reference-6), [7](#reference-7))

These documents establish a V6/V7 lineage and continuing peripheral support without proving a separate V7 board or an exact V7 launch date.

### Challenger Version 8

**Challenger V8**, principally identified by **TS0816**, became the longstanding platform against which later Challenger generations were compared. It was already documented in the mid-1990s: Tecom's 1998 radio-interface guide refers back to a Version 8 programming guide issued in August 1995, and an original October 1997 V8 user guide survives. ([7](#reference-7), [8](#reference-8))

Manufacturer specifications describe a modular system with **16 areas**, up to **256 inputs**, **16 remote arming stations**, **64 doors** and **255 relays**. Optional memory and intelligent access-control equipment expanded the system beyond its basic configuration. These are system maxima with appropriate expansion, rather than devices all wired directly to the main board. ([9](#reference-9))

V8 installations used remote keypads, input expanders and door or lift controllers. Its user guide also includes camera film-counter functions, reflecting the surveillance equipment with which some 1990s systems interacted. ([8](#reference-8))

V8 remained relevant well into the following decades. Monash University's 2015 security design standard specified Tecom, then identified with Interlogix, V8 equipment for its intrusion and access-control systems. This provides a documented example of institutional adoption, rather than relying solely on suppliers' market claims. ([10](#reference-10))

### Challenger10

**Challenger10** was introduced in **2013**. An April industry report described approximately fifteen months of development, led from April 2012 by former Tecom Systems managing director Dean Reilly. ([4](#reference-4))

The redesign moved from V8's 8-bit processor to a **32-bit processor**. Backward compatibility was an explicit design priority: the developers retained familiar programming methods and positioned mounting points and connectors to simplify replacement of a V8 main panel. V8 was still available at the time of the April 2013 report. ([4](#reference-4))

The TS1016 datasheet lists **99 areas**, **1,008 inputs**, **512 relays**, **32 remote arming stations** and two RS-485 buses. Standard capacity was **2,000 users**, expandable to **65,535** with the TS1084 module. Separate histories held **5,000 alarm events** and **5,000 access events**. ([18](#reference-18))

Onboard **Ethernet, USB, RS-232 and a telephone dialler**, SD-card configuration backup, remote firmware updating, stored text descriptions and multiple communications paths improved network integration and maintenance. ([18](#reference-18))

The July 2021 manufacturer notice formally superseded Challenger10 with ChallengerPlus for new orders. It also documented the ability to run Challenger10 firmware on ChallengerPlus hardware when required. This was a sales transition, not an immediate termination of every Challenger10 installation or firmware branch; a Challenger10 maintenance release followed in September 2023. ([21](#reference-21), [34](#reference-34))

### ChallengerSE and ChallengerLE

**ChallengerSE** and **ChallengerLE** appear in the installation manual revised on **20 August 2015**. ([19](#reference-19))

**ChallengerSE**, the **Standard Edition** (**TS1016SE**), initially supported 100 users, with expansion available. Ethernet, USB and RS-232 connections were time-restricted unless the enhanced-communications licence was installed. ([19](#reference-19))

**ChallengerLE**, the **Lite Edition** (**TS1016LE**), offered 100 users, 16 areas, eight onboard inputs and expansion through one DGP. It did not support the intelligent four-door or four-lift controllers used by larger systems. ([19](#reference-19))

The manual also lists **TS1016T**, a Challenger10 variant incorporating a mains transformer, rather than another panel generation. ([19](#reference-19))

### ChallengerPlus and ChallengerLEPlus

**ChallengerPlus** was released on **9 September 2019** with **V10-07.44900** firmware. It built on Challenger10, with an upgrade path for existing panels through CTPlus. ([20](#reference-20))

It added **UltraSync**, cloud updating, DHCP and support for the **Network Access Controller**, **Dual Wiegand Interface** and **4G module**. Up to 32 standard doors and two ten-floor standard lifts could be configured; those lifts did not require the older intelligent lift controller. ([20](#reference-20))

The initial release required updated compatible management software. ChallengerPlus replaced Challenger10 for new orders in July 2021. ([20](#reference-20), [21](#reference-21))

**ChallengerLEPlus** extended the smaller-panel branch into the Plus ecosystem. A manufacturer datasheet revision dated **29 April 2021** documents the product, although its original launch date was not established. Later documentation identifies it as **TS1016LEPLUS**. It retains the smaller system scale—100 users and 16 areas—while adding UltraSync and mobile-app functions, including push notifications. Ethernet is onboard, with cellular connectivity available through an optional module. ([22](#reference-22), [23](#reference-23))

### Tecom Discovery

**Tecom Discovery**, model **TSX10000**, was released on **26 August 2024**. It continued the ChallengerPlus system architecture while introducing new hardware, a responsive web interface and a DIN-rail-mounted polycarbonate/ABS housing. The release note specified 12/24-volt DC power input and an optional kit for using existing ChallengerPlus enclosures. ([24](#reference-24))

Discovery initially supported **CTPlus 3.0 or later** and **WMS Pro 2.0 or later**. Its compatibility was selective: the release note excluded the older TS0866, TS0867 and TS0869 intelligent controllers, together with TS1053, TS1054 and TS1084 expansion modules. Consequently, a Discovery migration could retain some Tecom equipment while requiring replacement of other components. ([24](#reference-24))

The **Discovery 2.0** firmware release in **November 2025** materially expanded the platform. It enabled onboard Wiegand reader functions, standard door and lift operation through the onboard reader ports, supported USB accessories, and full installer and user programming through the web interface. It also increased the default onboard capacity to **65,535 users**, without an additional licence, and added names/descriptions for all users and programming entities. ([25](#reference-25))

The September 2026 compatibility matrix lists Discovery with 99 areas, 1,008 inputs, three RS-485 buses and four onboard relays. It distinguishes Discovery's 65,535 onboard named users from ChallengerPlus's 2,000 onboard named users, expandable to 65,535 with a memory module. These figures describe the documented later firmware state, rather than necessarily every feature available at Discovery's initial launch. ([26](#reference-26))

## Corporate ownership and branding

Challenger retained its Tecom identity through several changes of ownership. This explains why manuals and equipment from the same broad product lineage carry Tecom Systems, Interlogix, GE, UTC, Carrier or Aritech names.

The late-1990s transition is less completely documented than the later corporate transactions. In a published professional history, former Sentrol manager Magnus Jonsson identifies the acquisition of Tecom in Australia among his activities during **April 1998–October 1999**. This places the acquisition in that period but does not establish its exact completion date. His account also associates the group's regional product strategies with ATS in Europe, Alliance in the United States and Challenger in Australia. ([12](#reference-12))

Australian Business Register records subsequently associate the Tecom Systems name with the Australian business that traded under SLC Technologies and then Interlogix. The register records the following legal-entity names for **ABN 84 086 771 404**. ([11](#reference-11))

| Effective date in the Australian register | Entity name |
| --- | --- |
| 9 February 2000 | SLC Technologies (Australia) Pty Ltd |
| 31 August 2001 | Interlogix Australia Pty Limited |
| 2 August 2002 | GE Interlogix Pty Limited |
| 16 June 2005 | GE Infrastructure Security Pty Limited |
| 24 July 2006 | GE Security Pty Ltd |
| 26 September 2012 | UTC Fire & Security Australia Pty Ltd |
| 19 September 2020 | Carrier Fire & Security Australia Pty Ltd |
| 21 February 2025 | KGS Fire & Security Australia Pty Ltd |

These are dates of recorded Australian entity names, which can differ from acquisition dates. The original Tecom Systems company identified in the 1993 manual had a different ACN. ([2](#reference-2), [11](#reference-11))

The major later group-level changes were:

- **21 February 2002:** General Electric completed its acquisition of Interlogix. ([13](#reference-13))
- **1 March 2010:** United Technologies announced completion of its acquisition of GE Security. The Interlogix name subsequently continued to appear on Challenger products, including Challenger10 and the initial ChallengerPlus release. ([14](#reference-14), [18](#reference-18), [20](#reference-20))
- **3 April 2020:** Carrier became an independent publicly traded company following its separation from United Technologies. ([15](#reference-15))
- **October 2020:** Carrier announced consolidation of its Interlogix intrusion and video offering under the **Aritech** brand. ChallengerPlus and TecomC4 were included in the regional offering discussed at the time. ([16](#reference-16))
- **2 December 2024:** An affiliate of **Lone Star Funds** completed its acquisition of Carrier's commercial and residential fire business, forming **Kidde Global Solutions**. The acquired business included Aritech. ([17](#reference-17))

As of September 2026, the Australian Tecom range is presented through Aritech under Kidde Global Solutions. The brand history is therefore a continuation of the Australian Tecom product family through successive corporate groups. ([11](#reference-11), [30](#reference-30))

## System architecture and software

### Main panel and distributed equipment

Challenger connects equipment distributed around a building. A **RAS** is a remote arming station, commonly a keypad or reader interface; a **DGP** is a data-gathering panel connecting additional field devices. ([8](#reference-8), [9](#reference-9))

The traditional Challenger **LAN** is an RS-485 peripheral bus, distinct from the Ethernet network used for software and reporting connections on later panels. ([9](#reference-9), [18](#reference-18))

The **Network Access Controller (NAC)** extended distributed access-control processing, allowing direct connection to management software or operation through ChallengerPlus. ([30](#reference-30))

### Communications and remote operation

In 1998, the **TS2053 radio packet interface** used Telstra's digital data network for alarm and status reporting. It illustrates the communications technology used before the later Ethernet and UltraSync generations. ([7](#reference-7))

The **TecomPlus** mobile application added phone-based area arming, door operation and event viewing through UltraSync. ([26](#reference-26))

### Management and configuration software

The software history comprises overlapping products with different purposes. An installer configuration tool, an operator's multi-site management system and a mobile application are not interchangeable panel generations.

| Software | Role in the Tecom ecosystem |
| --- | --- |
| **Titan** | Established PC software used with earlier Challenger systems; Challenger10 documentation also describes its use for remote firmware updating. ([18](#reference-18)) |
| **Forcefield** | Integrated operator platform combining access control, intrusion and video functions. It remained listed in the September 2026 compatibility matrix. ([26](#reference-26), [30](#reference-30)) |
| **Security Commander** | Earlier management software. Base/professional licences ended sale on 31 March 2020, other licences on 31 December 2020, and all Security Commander products reached end of support on 31 December 2021. ([29](#reference-29)) |
| **CTPlus** | Installer tool for programming, configuration transfer, backup, remote maintenance and diagnostics. It also became the documented upgrade route from Challenger10 to ChallengerPlus. ([20](#reference-20), [31](#reference-31)) |
| **TecomC4** | Open management platform covering intrusion, access control and video. Aritech announced end of sale for new installations in 2026, explicitly excluding existing licensed installations from that notice. ([30](#reference-30), [33](#reference-33)) |
| **Web Management System (WMS)** | Web-based reporting tool associated with Challenger10; distinct from the later WMS Pro management suite. ([30](#reference-30)) |
| **WMS Pro** | Web-interface management suite for users, access rights, alarms and sites, with functions including maps, reporting and automation. Discovery's original release required WMS Pro 2.0 or later when using that software. ([24](#reference-24), [29](#reference-29), [32](#reference-32)) |

Software compatibility differs between generations. The September 2026 matrix lists Discovery with CTPlus and WMS Pro, while Forcefield supports specified other Tecom panels. ([26](#reference-26))

## Adoption, continuity and retirement

The long life of the V8 generation is visible in both customer and manufacturer records: it appeared in Monash University's 2015 requirements, and Aritech's eventual retirement notice described the panel as having been discontinued for more than a decade before support ended. ([10](#reference-10), [27](#reference-27))

Two later retirement milestones are particularly significant:

- **1 October 2024:** Aritech ended support for **Challenger V8** through Aritech and its distribution network. The notice recommended migration to ChallengerPlus or Discovery. This was the end of support, not the original end-of-sale date. ([27](#reference-27))
- **1 December 2025:** The **TS0866, TS0867 and TS0869** V8 controller family reached end of life. Aritech stated that applicable warranties would still be honoured. ([28](#reference-28))

The September 2026 compatibility matrix documents Challenger10, Plus, LEPlus and Discovery together. This continuing overlap illustrates the gradual transition between generations. ([26](#reference-26))

## Historical record and dating limitations

The strongest evidence for this history comes from dated manufacturer manuals, release notes, official lifecycle notices, corporate announcements and the Australian Business Register. Contemporary industry reporting and a documented customer standard provide additional context. Some older primary documents survive only on third-party manual archives or installer websites.

Three gaps remain in the accessible record:

1. **The first release:** 1989 is consistently reported in retrospective commercial descriptions, but an original 1989 launch document was not located.
2. **The earliest numbered versions:** the research did not establish a complete release history for Versions 1–5, an independently marketed V7 hardware board, or a distinct Challenger9 product. Missing evidence should not be interpreted as proof that no internal or limited-release version existed.
3. **Some variant launch dates:** the dates given for SE, LE and LEPlus establish that they existed by the cited documentation dates; they are not asserted to be their first sale dates.

Document issue dates have been taken from the documents themselves where available. A PDF's scan date, a website upload folder or a manual archive's posting date can be years later than the original publication. Likewise, later firmware capabilities have not been assumed to exist at a panel's initial launch.
